# BAES Author — Technical Profile v0.1

**Author:** Babak Rasti M. (بابک راستی میمندی)

## Profile

Babak Rasti M. is a Software Engineer, Systems Architect, and Independent Researcher in Human–AI Engineering with 28 years of hands-on experience in software engineering and architecture.

He is the **Creator and Principal Developer of BAES (Babak AI Engineering Standard)**.

He also has approximately 10 years of operational IT management experience as a former Hospital IT Manager.

## Technical Interests

His current technical interests include:

- Software Engineering
- Systems Architecture
- Human–AI Engineering
- AI Engineering
- Agentic and Autonomous AI Systems
- Legacy and Long-lived Systems
- Distributed and Reliable Systems

## Engineering Focus

A central concern in his current work is the engineering boundary between:

**human intent → delegation → AI investigation/reasoning → evidence → challenge or recommendation → human decision → authorized execution → result → traceability**

This sequence is a conceptual representation used by BAES; it is not presented as a mandatory implementation workflow.

The technical questions of particular interest include how AI-intensive systems represent and preserve distinctions between intent, reasoning, recommendation, decision, authority, execution, conditions, revocation or supersession, and traceability.

## Technology-Neutral Position

The BAES work is intentionally independent of a particular model, agent framework, programming language, cloud platform, orchestration library, identity system, authorization product, or observability stack.

The purpose of this technical profile is to describe the author's engineering context. It does not claim that BAES is required for agentic, autonomous, enterprise, or other AI systems.

## External Technical Review

The author welcomes technical review concerning:

- conceptual redundancy or ambiguity;
- interaction with existing engineering practices;
- agent and tool-using system boundaries;
- authorization versus capability;
- recommendation versus decision;
- execution attribution;
- traceability;
- practical overhead;
- failure and boundary conditions;
- contexts in which the proposed distinctions do not provide sufficient value.
